title: Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Boston College (Carroll School of Mgmt) - Nov 3, 2016
summary: Pabrai presents his 'quest for 10-100 baggers' framework, motivated by his 1994-95 experience with Satyam, Blue Dart and Kotak in India and CMGI, where he repeatedly bought future multi-baggers but sold far too early. He lays out five categories of businesses that can become huge multi-baggers (idiot-proof moats, moats needing competent managers, risk-vs-uncertainty confusion, bankruptcies/special situations, and upside-without-downside) with case studies including IPSCO, Fiat Chrysler, Tesoro, Frontline, Teck Cominco, Covanta and Silicon Valley Bank. Q&A covers selling discipline, circle of competence, Apple, GM's captive finance arm, career alignment and resilience.

ideas.idea: The classic buy-at-50-cents, sell-at-90-cents value approach is flawed because it forces you out of the rare multi-baggers that drive most long-term wealth.
ideas.detail: For over two decades he bought at 50 cents on the dollar and sold at 90 cents, expecting convergence in 2-3 years (a 30%+ or low-to-mid 20s return). Looking back, he found many cases where he made a 2x-4x, sold, and the stock then went up 10x.

ideas.idea: Each investor gets a limited quota of truly great businesses in a lifetime; the key is to recognize when one is in your portfolio and not be in a hurry to act.
ideas.detail: He credits Charlie Munger with this observation. The best action when you own such a business is 'to take an afternoon nap, not put a sell order in.'

ideas.idea: Accidentally holding 100 shares of Blue Dart for 21 years turned about $100 into $11,000, showing what buy-and-hold could have done with his whole India basket.
ideas.detail: In 1994-95 he put $30,000 of a $1 million portfolio into four Indian stocks. Satyam went from ~45 rupees to ~7,000 (100x, $15k to $1.5M, sold near the 2000 peak); had he held, Blue Dart would have been a 60x ($7,700 to $465,000) and Kotak a 50x ($1,500 to $75,000); Skypack lost half.

ideas.idea: Long holding periods are doubly valuable because deferred capital gains taxes act as a free loan from the government for the whole period.
ideas.detail: Holding for 10-30 years and paying tax once is like investing in a retirement account. In California his marginal state rate is north of 12% on top of ~20-22% federal long-term gains, so deferral matters even more.

ideas.idea: Category 1 multi-baggers are businesses with such wide, deep moats that idiots can run them; they rarely get cheap enough for a cheapskate to buy.
ideas.detail: Examples: Coca-Cola, See's Candies, Moody's, Visa, MasterCard, American Express, beer and tobacco companies (human vices). Coke grew nonstop for 125 years despite decades of poor managers. He admits he almost never owns these because he shops the bargain bin.

ideas.idea: If the 2008 financial crisis could not destroy Moody's moat, nothing will; a moat that survives its worst-case seismic event is the ultimate one to own.
ideas.detail: Moody's charges 10-30x its cost to rate debt; an analyst paid $200k brings in ~$5M revenue; there are 50,000+ rated debt instruments vs ~5,000 stocks. Despite selling 'poison ratings' in 2008, fines and regulatory attack, the stock went from a $60 2007 high to nearly double. He regrets navel-gazing instead of buying in 2008-10 and says next time he will call his broker.

ideas.idea: Guy Spier's model: identify a great US business (Coke bottlers, Moody's) and then hunt for its analogues in other countries where the market may not have priced the same economics.
ideas.detail: Applying this, Spier bought CRISIL in India in 2001-02 and added in 2004-05, then sold after 2-3x. The 2001 purchase is now up 200x and the 2005 purchase 43x; untouched, it alone would be ~$150-160M, roughly 50% of his ~$160M fund. S&P/McGraw Hill paid $8.5M for 10% of CRISIL in 1998 at an $85M market cap; CRISIL is now ~$25B and S&P owns ~75%. Even at CRISIL's nosebleed P/E today, Pabrai says it would probably be a mistake to sell, since Indian debt instruments in 10-50 years will dwarf today's.

ideas.idea: Category 2 multi-baggers are great franchises that need competent, non-idiot managers; they are more common than category 1 but their moats are less robust.
ideas.detail: Examples: Amazon, Costco, Geico, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Blue Dart, Satyam, Restaurant Brands International, Yum Brands, Domino's, Marriott (which owns under 1% of the hotels carrying its brands yet gets a cut of every night's stay). He owned three of these (Kotak, Blue Dart, Satyam) and was not smart enough to keep two of them.

ideas.idea: Category 3, the one that shows up most in his portfolio, is where the market confuses risk with uncertainty: low risk of permanent loss but high uncertainty about outcomes gets punished with a very low price.
ideas.detail: IPSCO in 2005 had a $2.5B market cap, $900M cash and ~$650M/yr of visible earnings for two years ($2.2B total) with no visibility beyond; he held it from ~$40 until a Swedish buyout at ~$160 in early 2007. Markets 'don't have much respect for companies with volatile earnings.'

ideas.idea: Fiat Chrysler is a current IPSCO-like 'set it and forget it' bet: a sub-$10B market cap against management's guidance of $5.50+ EPS and net-cash balance sheet in 2018.
ideas.detail: Stock under $7 vs guided 2018 EPS of $5.50 implies ~1.3x P/E; management guides 2018 EBIT over 9B euros while the street models ~3B. The 2014-2018 plan has been delivered 'in spades' for three years; Jeep output rose from ~250k in 2009 to ~1.4M in 2016 with China targeted at 500k by 2018. He admits a 'man crush' on CEO Sergio Marchionne clouds his view and stresses it is not a stock tip. Of Value Line's 1,700 companies usually only one or two trade below a P/E of two.

ideas.idea: Cyclical businesses run by gifted managers can become 30-200 baggers from the trough, so 'take the double and leave' in a cyclical can be a costly mistake.
ideas.detail: He bought Tesoro in mid-2002 at $7.50 (down from $30; $480M market cap vs >$1B estimated value), watched it fall to $1.33 ($85M market cap), held, and sold at $15 for a 100% gain. Tesoro's market cap is now $10B plus a $6B Tesoro Logistics spin-off and dividends exceeding the original market cap; 200x from the bottom tick and 30x+ from his price. He under-appreciated CEO Bruce Smith. He also notes US refining is not a pure commodity: no new refinery in 30 years (NIMBY) and state-specific blends make each refinery unique.

ideas.idea: Shipping's boom-bust cycle is structural: ship owners project present rates to infinity, order ships at peak rates, and the 3-4 year build lag means new supply arrives together and crushes rates, which triggers scrapping and sets up the next boom.
ideas.detail: VLCC spot rates range from $5-6k/day (loss-making) to $300k+/day; above $30k the company makes a lot of money. Old rust-buckets get scrapped for 10-20% of original cost when rates collapse, and after Exxon Valdez (1992 double-hull mandate) single hulls were scrapped even faster. Same dynamic as class-A office buildings.

ideas.idea: Selling Frontline at 90% of liquidation value was a mistake born of a juvenile understanding of human nature's swings; with 'Frontline 2.0' he will ride past liquidation value.
ideas.detail: Bought Frontline in 2002 at ~$6 against ~$9 liquidation value with debt at the ship level (lenders could only repossess ships). Had he held, $56 in dividends plus the Ship Finance spin-off ($24 in dividends, $14 stock) would have made ~$130, nearly 25x. He has found an unnamed shipping company trading at half liquidation value that he is now researching. This time, once it doubles he may take the principal off and let the rest ride with a taper, since a cyclical is not a Coke and will crash and burn someday.

ideas.idea: Blue-chip cyclicals with bridge-loan overhangs can collapse 90% in weeks because their natural 'widows and orphans' shareholder base flees; banks would rather extend and pretend than liquidate.
ideas.detail: Teck Cominco fell from $45 to $4 in 10-12 weeks in 2008 after a debt-funded metallurgical coal acquisition. He bought under $5 as a 2% bet in a basket of commodity plays (no losers), a Chinese strategic investor bought a stake two months later, and he sold at ~$35 for a 7x in a year before it hit $55. He missed the repeat opportunity when it fell below $5 again in early 2016.

ideas.idea: Category 4 is bankruptcies, reorganizations, public LBOs and special situations, where tax-code masters like Sam Zell create unusual dynamics.
ideas.detail: Zell bought bankrupt Mission Insurance's $650M of NOLs for $30M, renamed it Danielson Holdings (Marty Whitman chairman), married it to a barge company that then went bankrupt ('bankruptcy to the power of bankruptcy'), then bought a waste-to-energy business that became Covanta. Pabrai bought at ~$9 via two rights offerings and sold in 18 months for ~90%; holding would have been a 4x. He names Buffett, Jay Pritzker, Zell and Leucadia as tax-code experts.

ideas.idea: Category 5 is 'upside without downside': a solid business at a modest price that carries a free, undisclosed moonshot option.
ideas.detail: In 1999 Silicon Valley Bank traded at a modest premium to book while holding undisclosed warrants from its venture-backed borrowers. He bought at $10-12, captured ~2.5x in about 2.5 years, and the stock went 4x. CMGI in his personal portfolio (10% of $1M, bought near book, sold for 100x) was similar.

ideas.idea: International cloning is possible even without 13Fs, via Indian broker disclosures of 1%+ holders and Bloomberg shareholder data for Korea and China.
ideas.detail: India requires brokers to disclose anyone owning over 1% of a public company; he subscribes to Alpha Ideas which compiles this quarterly. He has found Korean and Chinese investments owned by investors he admires this way.

ideas.idea: You do not need an opinion on everything; put hard questions like the trajectory of oil demand in the 'too hard' pile and bet only on high-probability events.
ideas.detail: He is confident tire volumes will be 20-40% higher in 2025 than 2016 but cannot say whether crude consumption will rise or fall. Buffett keeps a physical 'too hard' box on his desk; on a visit Pabrai found it empty and Buffett filled it with papers for a photo.

ideas.idea: Munger's grocery-store approach (find what you love, wait for it to go on sale) beats Graham's (buy whatever is most discounted), though Pabrai admits he can never bring himself to pay full price for a great business.
ideas.detail: He praises Tom Russo and Tom Gayner for playing only in categories 1 and 2, with the mild critique that Russo shows less price discipline. Buffett called not selling Coke at 40x earnings in 1999-2000 a mistake in hindsight, but Berkshire will likely hold Coke for decades more, which may be wise.

ideas.idea: He now owns one category-1 'can be run by idiots' business for the first time and has decided never to sell it; even at 10x he would not sell.
ideas.detail: He believes its moat will exist 100 and possibly 300 years from now; he will leave it alone and play his 'Mickey Mouse games' with shipping companies separately. If it reached 50x in his lifetime he still would not sell at 10x.

ideas.idea: To ask whether something is in your circle of competence is to answer it: if you are wondering, it is not.
ideas.detail: He attributes this to Charlie Munger and adds that in investing you want absolute no-brainers; any doubt means you should not go there.

ideas.idea: Passing on Apple in 2007 despite an eloquent pitch about the app store and changing human habits was a costly blind spot caused by refusing anything above a single-digit P/E.
ideas.detail: A VC friend and fund investor explained the iPhone ecosystem and 'habit economy' in 2007. In 2016 Apple trades at under 12-13x earnings ex-cash with unit sales dropping but earnings rising because over a billion devices carry apps; he still finds a shipping company at half liquidation value more tangible than Apple at 12x, which 'may be a mistake but is the way I'm wired.'

ideas.idea: Pick investing as a calling only if you would do it for a schoolteacher's pay; your external life must align with your internal wiring or you will not go far.
ideas.detail: In 1999, via YPO, industrial psychologists did a 360 analysis and gave him a 20-page 'owner's manual' at age 34 for $2,000, concluding that running his 170-person IT company was far from his wiring while Pabrai Funds fit perfectly. One psychologist became an early fund investor because he had 'cracked your brain open.' He recommends Jiro Dreams of Sushi and Life is Beautiful.

ideas.idea: Suffering comes from our reaction to events, not the events themselves, so down-and-out periods should be treated as temporary conditions like collapsed shipping rates.
ideas.detail: His parents went through multiple bankruptcies in his childhood yet his mother never got depressed; his father paid a Hindu astrologer he knew was a fraud because 'he is my rope' out of the well. He cites 'if wealth is lost nothing is lost, if health is lost something is lost, if character is lost everything is lost.'

ideas.idea: Captive finance arms of manufacturers like John Deere, Ford and GM are remarkably stable, earning more nearly every year even through 2008-10, and deserve at least 15x earnings.
ideas.detail: John Deere's finance arm has made money every year since 1992 in a nearly straight line while equipment earnings swung. GM Financial earns ~$1B, guided to $2B in a few years (worth ~$30B) and GM's China JV produces ~$2B a year like clockwork; together ~$4B is worth at least $60B, yet GM trades under $50B with $20B cash, ignoring trucks, Cadillac and parts. That is why he owns GM. He adds that the market is there to serve you, not instruct you: value is its own catalyst and he has never done catalyst investing.
